extracted.intended_audience: students, mathematicians, and natural philosophers studying classical mechanics and mathematical methods (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometrical and physical principles and lemmas from a classical mechanics treatise (Newton's Principia): laws of motion, corollaries about collisions and center of gravity, method-of-limits lemmas for areas/arcs/ratios, and theorems on centripetal forces and time-area relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Law (Action and Reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action and its contrary reaction are equal (Law 3): for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via collisions and reflected in Corollaries and experiments (pendula). Demonstrated by collision examples (spherical bodies, unequal masses), elastic and imperfectly elastic cases; experimental confirmation by pendulum collisions (Marriott, Wren, Wallis, Huygens referenced). Notes on elasticity: perfectly elastic bodies return with relative velocity equal to the incident relative velocity; imperfect elasticity reduces return velocity in determinate proportion to elastic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of quantity of motion (momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of motion collected by taking the sum of motions to the same part and the difference of motions to contrary parts is not changed by the mutual action of bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated from Law 3 and Law 2; illustrated with numerical examples of colliding spheres (assignment of 'parts' of motion before and after). Used to compute post-collision velocities by conserving the signed sum of motion-parts. Emphasizes experimental agreement within measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of gravity unaffected by internal actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The common center of gravity of bodies is not altered in its state of motion or rest by the internal actions of the bodies on one another; hence, absent external forces the center either remains at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by pairwise action analysis and inductive composition for many bodies. Used to reduce the motion of a system to motion of its center; implies system inertia law analogous to single body. Applies equally in plane and solid space (Lemma referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of uniform motion (motions in a uniformly moving vessel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies contained in a given space have the same motions among themselves whether the space is at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line (no effect of uniform translation on internal motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corol. V: proven by showing equal sums/differences of motions lead to same effects of collisions; confirmed by ship experiments. Used as practical experimental principle: motions behave identically aboard a uniformly moving ship or a stationar y one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal parallel accelerative forces preserve relative motion
rubrics_metrics.description: If bodies are moved among themselves and urged by equal accelerative forces in parallel lines, they will continue to move among themselves as if those equal forces were not applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corol. VI: since equal parallel accelerations produce equal velocities (per Law 2) the relative positions/motions of bodies are unchanged. This provides superposition-style reasoning for adding uniform accelerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical advantage: velocities reciprocal to forces
rubrics_metrics.description: In machines, forces and velocities are reciprocal: where agent and resistent velocities are reciprocally proportional, the forces balance; conversely, given reciprocal velocities the agent sustains the resistance. Examples include levers, pulleys (trochlea/polyspaston), screws (cochlea), wedges and mallet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by geometric decomposition of oblique planes, wedges, cochlea; used to solve problems 'given weight and force, find required velocities' (Datum pondus data vi movendi ...). Practical note: efficacy of machines consists in decreasing velocity to increase force and vice versa. Also notes on overcoming friction/cohesion: if velocity disparity is large enough to overcome resistances, surplus force accelerates the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experiments (pendula) to test theoretical laws and account for resistances
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendulum collisions used to test Law 3 and reflections: measure pre- and post-collision motions using chords of arcs and correct for air resistance and imperfect elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed experimental procedure: drop pendula from given arc points, measure return points after one oscillation, correct using quarter parts of retardation ascribed to air resistance, reconstruct vacuo velocities by using chord approximations. Notes on measurement errors (three digits, difficulty with simultaneous drops) and material-dependent restitution ratios (wool ~5:9, steel similar, cork less, glass ~15:16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of ultimate ratios (limits) — foundational lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If quantities, or ratios of quantities, constantly tend to equality over time (i.e., can approach each other arbitrarily closely), then in the limit they are equal (Lemma I and Scholium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the basis for reasoning about evanescent (vanishing) quantities: interpret 'ultimate ratio' as limit ratio at vanishing size. Rejects indivisibles hypothesis as harsher; prescribes using limits as properly geometric. Addresses objections about inexistence of ultimate quantities by defining ultimate ratio as the ratio 'when they vanish'—i.e., the limiting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area approximation by inscribed and circumscribed parallelograms (limit equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a curve is approximated by inscribed and circumscribed parallelograms under equal bases and diminishing widths, the ultimate ratios of the inscribed figure, the circumscribed figure, and the intermediate curvilinear figure are equal (Lemma II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proves that the difference rectangle becomes arbitrarily small as width diminishes; combines with Lemma I to assert equality of limiting areas. Used to justify replacing sums of infinitesimal parallelograms by the exact curved area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal widths also yield equal ultimate ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the parallelograms' widths (latitudes) are unequal, provided they all diminish to zero, the ultimate ratios of inscribed/circumscribed approximations still equal the curve (Lemma III).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs a maximal-latitude parallelogram to bound the difference and appeals to Lemma I to conclude equality in the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termwise ultimate ratio equality implies figure ratio equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If two figures have series of parallelograms inscribed with the same number and the ultimate ratios of corresponding parallelograms are equal term-by-term, then the two whole figures are in that same ultimate ratio (Lemma IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composes termwise proportionality into total proportionality via sums; used to compare complex figures by comparing infinitesimal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and area scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: All corresponding sides of similar figures (curvilinear or rectilinear) are proportional, and areas are in the duplicate (square) ratio of corresponding sides (Lemma V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends similarity notions to limit/curvilinear figures and justifies area scaling by square of linear scale factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle between chord and tangent vanishes in the limit
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve and chord AB with tangent at A, as point B approaches A the angle BAD (between chord and tangent) diminishes indefinitely and in the limit vanishes (Lemma VI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument via extension of chord and tangent and exclusion of impossible geometry; used to justify treating chord and tangent as coincident in the infinitesimal limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate ratio equality of arc, chord, and tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate ratio of an arc, its chord, and the tangent at the endpoint are equal as the arc vanishes (Lemma VII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses similarity of infinitesimal constructions and Lemma VI to equate limiting lengths; corollaries extend to ratios of abscissas, chords, arcs, and allow interchange of these elements in limit arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degenerate triangles become similar in the limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Three triangles formed by a chord, tangent, and given lines approach a form of similarity as their defining points coalesce; the ultimate form is similarity (Lemma VIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to substitute infinitesimal triangles for one another in limiting ratio arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of triangles with ordinate applications scale as square of sides
rubrics_metrics.description: If a given straight line and a curve meet, and ordinates (perpendiculars) are applied to the straight line at given angles, the areas of the resulting triangles are in the duplicate ratio of the sides (Lemma IX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs proportional ordinates and passes to the limit by shrinking arcs; used to relate areas under curves to linear dimensions and to derive time-space relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces under regular force proportional to square of times
rubrics_metrics.description: The spaces that a body describes under any regular (uniformly varying) force are in the duplicate (square) ratio of the times employed (Lemma X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses times as straight lines, velocities as ordinates, and spaces as areas under the velocity-time curve; corollaries: errors under similar bodies with proportional forces scale with squares of times and with forces × time^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtending vanishing contact-angle and chord-square relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The vanishing subtended angle at the point of contact is ultimately in the duplicate ratio of the subtending arc's measure; corollaries: squares of sines/chords behave as duplicate ratios of small arcs and relate to triangles and parabolic segment areas (Lemma XI and corollaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases handle perpendiculars to tangents and general inclination; leads to consequences about triangular area scaling (triplicate and sesquiplicate ratios) and specific relations for parabolic segments (areas being two-thirds of certain triangles). Provides basis for replacing curvilinear segments by algebraic proportions in limit arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled use of limits vs indivisibles (Scholium guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should employ limits (ultimately vanishing quantities and their limiting ratios) rather than the harder indivisibles hypothesis; interpret 'ultimate' and 'first' ratios as the limits as quantities vanish or begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains philosophical and methodological position: limits have definite meaning; answers objections about inexistence of ultimate magnitudes by clarifying that ultimate ratio is the limiting ratio at the instant of vanishing. Advises reading infinitesimal talk as limits and refers readers to earlier lemmas when using 'evanescent' parts in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas described by radius vectors are proportional to time (Kepler-area-law style theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moves under forces directed to an immobile centre, the areas described by the radius to that center are proportional to the times (Proposition I, Theorem I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof: divide time in equal parts, show equal areas traced in equal times when centripetal impulses act at the interval endpoints; passing to the limit with infinitely small time parts gives continuous motion result. Corollary: if areas are not proportional to times in a medium, forces do not all point to the same center; conversely, accelerated area description indicates non-central forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of centripetal force when radius-area proportionality holds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moving in a curve, with radius drawn to a point (immobile or moving uniformly), describes areas about that point proportional to times, then it is urged by a centripetal force towards that point (Proposition II, Theorem II — beginning in this chunk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begins with the converse: observed area-time proportionality implies a central attractive force; the proof proceeds by discrete impulse approximation and passage to the limit (continuation beyond current chunk).
